en: The Poem on the Arising of the Buddha composed by the teacher Śāntibhikṣu; the first section.
He who, moist with affection, constantly extends happiness to those suffering in life; he who, through loving-kindness, bestows vast fearlessness upon the minds of living beings;
he in whom the trusting people here find joy as if in a mother—[he is a true friend].
May that certain supreme being, who possesses the essence of the nectar of compassion, be victorious! ||1||
He who, with a soul filled with supreme affection, bestowed a boon upon the world; he who, for the welfare of living beings, extracts the thorns from the path of life;
and because of whose noble intention the world never receives the arrows of curses—[to him I bow].
I worship that Bodhisattva for the sake of fulfilling all the hopes of the world.
He who, having relied upon Dīpaṃkara, formed a noble resolve for awakening, and obtained from Śrīghana the boon, "You shall succeed in your own heart's desires"—
he who thus possessed such an aspiration and set out with compassion was prophesied.
May that Blessed One, who was born in the Śākya clan, always ordain our well-being. ||3||
That which is eternally sustained, that which is perceived by the mind, which is untainted, eternal, composed of Dharma, immeasurable, and endowed with a treasury of compassion—
it is by the power of this alone that a person remains capable and free from violence.
For the sake of peace for all worlds, I worship that form of the Blessed One, whose sole essence is peace. ||4||
By her splendor, she eclipsed the beauty of the beloved Rati’s body as manifested through her emanations;
by the power of her own gentleness, she robbed the moonlight of its luster from the moon;
and with the honey of her eloquent speech, she sprinkled the bitter minds of people with sweetness.
I worship the body of the Blessed One, peerless in form, whose sole essence is radiant beauty. 5.
How peaceful is enmity! Oh, how the tigress nourishes the fawns with her milk; oh, even the sun does not cause distress with its scorching rays as it licks them;
alas, the multitude of worlds, divided by disputes and quarrels, now attains unity today.
"Behold, O friends, the arising of the Buddha, by which this entire agitated world is pacified!
Having heard these most enchanting and pleasing words spoken by the illustrious Brahmā,
the gods, assuming human forms, arrived from all sides at the glorious Lumbinī on earth.
Making the people glorious with their most beautiful and reddish-pink colored powders,
they dance and spread the splendor of song, sweet with the flow of aesthetic sentiments and expressions.
Out of compassion for this world, which is without a protector, given to disputation, delighting in strife, and not practicing what is wholesome, he has descended to earth.
I pay homage to the Lord of the World!
I pay homage to the Lord of the World, who perceives the world as consisting of the distinction between self and other, and who has descended into the worlds in order to unite them. ||a||
Having descended out of compassion in order to instruct those who harm living beings for the sake of dharma, and those who harm the world for the sake of sovereignty.
I pay homage to the Lord of the World. ||i||
He who does not strike with punishment, who protects by means of the Dharma without weapons—
he has descended [into this world] to be called the Protector.
I pay homage to the Lord of the World. ||ī||
Though a slave to craving and never full, man appears as if always filled with wealth;
you have descended to teach the bliss of tranquility.
I pay homage to the Lord of the World. Om.
To one who here steals the property of others out of craving and behaves improperly toward the wives of others,
he has indeed descended to teach moral conduct.
I pay homage to the Lord of the World. Ū.
And that effort which is applied to removing one's own suffering—
that same effort he has descended [into this world] to declare should also be applied to removing the suffering of others.
I pay homage to the Lord of the World. ||ṛ||
His conduct makes even a person with a compassionate mind entirely pure by a mere fraction;
thus he descended into the world to teach this.
I pay homage to the Lord of the World. Ṛ.
Adorned with garments of lovely hue like the glow of the dawn,
and possessing blossoming *palāśa* leaves as enchanting as the laughter of a most youthful fire;
Madhurī here worships the Lord of Beings;
O remover of grief, by your own compassion, make me too—who am bowed before you—your protégé. (a)
In every direction, with *sāla* trees in full bloom, most effectively wafting forth fragrant scents,
and with *rasāla* trees beautiful with the warbling of birds delighted by fresh blossoms;
Madhurī here worships the Lord of Beings;
O Dispeller of Sorrow, by Your own compassion, make me too—who am bowed before You—possessed of a protector. (Ā)
By the pleasant conversations of young men who delight in wandering through the avenues of *vakula* trees,
and by the many playful words uttered during the games of children gathered in the mango groves;
Madhurī here worships the Lord of Beings;
O Dispeller of Sorrow, by your own compassion, make me too—who am bowed before you—possessed of a protector. ||i||
Here, sweetness honors the Lord of Men with the gentle songs of peasant women bending under the harvest of barley, wheat, and grain,
and with the expansion of musical performances augmented by the shouts of approval from the young people who have been given gifts.
O remover of sorrow, by your own compassion, make me too—who bows before you—possessed of a protector. ||ī||

With the bodies of people swinging on swings suspended from banyan and tamarind trees, and with those who, having captivated hearts during this season of abundance, were overcome by the most intense sentiments of fear and heroism;
Madhurī here worships the Lord of Beings;
O Dispeller of Sorrow, by Your own compassion, make me too—who am bowed before You—possessed of a protector. ||u||

[The forest was filled] with bees greedy for honey, beautiful in their flight, making humming sounds as they flapped their wings; agitated and dwelling within the interior of flower-houses submerged in a mass of nectar.
Madhurī here worships the Lord of Beings;
O Dispeller of Sorrow, by Your own compassion, make me too—who am bowed before You—possessed of a protector. (Ū)
Having dispelled the harshness of mind with the most exquisitely charming sentiments and moods, and with the sweet,
melodious warbling of the cuckoo— a sound that reaches the hearts of all people— [he spoke].
Madhurī will surely bring the Lord of Men here;
O Dispeller of Sorrow, by your own compassion, make me too—who am bowed before you—your protégé. (Ṛ)
By the breezes, supremely skilled in causing the blossoming of the lovely Lumbinī grove, which are steadfast in their intent to produce horripilation upon the body through the pleasure of touch;
||| By those winds most expert in the unfolding of the charming forest of Lumbinī, whose purpose it was to bring about the bristling of hair on the skin through the bliss of contact; |||
Madhurī here worships the Lord of Beings;
O Dispeller of Sorrow, by Your own compassion, make me too—who am bowed before You—possessed of a protector. ||Ṛ||
By your most meritorious birth here, [the world] was as [enlightened] by the rising of the sun, the jewel of the sky.
May there be success; may there be auspiciousness for all people. May there be prosperity; may there be auspiciousness for all people. ||a||
Just as the breath of this world is restored by the wind that gives life, so may all the auspiciousness of every person be accomplished through your rising.
May there be prosperity for all people; may there be auspiciousness! Ā!
Like food is to the life of the world,
so you are through your nature as the cause of its revival.
May there be success for all people;
may there be prosperity for all people. ||i||
It was like the happiness felt when the god who rains at the proper time pours down rain, or as it is by your timely dispensation of the Dharma.
May there be success; may there be auspiciousness for all people. May there be prosperity; may there be auspiciousness for all people. ||ī||
It was as if the spring season had broken into a smile of blossoms,
brought about by the joy that arose within you.
May there be success; may there be auspiciousness for all people. May there be prosperity; may there be auspiciousness for all people. ||u||
Like a great flood,
it was as if by the arising of your compassion.
May there be success; may there be auspiciousness for all people. May there be prosperity; may there be auspiciousness for all people. || ū ||
Like the refinement of the body by means of an alchemical elixir,
[it was brought about] by the arising of that which dispels your suffering.
May there be success; may there be auspiciousness for all people. May there be prosperity; may there be auspiciousness for all people. ||Ṛ||
Like the sky by which all people travel,
so it is by you who have arisen as a refuge.
May there be success; may there be the auspiciousness of all people. May there be prosperity; may there be the auspiciousness of all people. Ṛ.
With songs accompanied by the flourishing of instrumental music, enriched with the seven notes arising from the throat;
with dances featuring expressive gestures and moving hands and feet, and glances from the corners of the eyes;
and with the actions of beautiful women made resonant by rhythmic clapping—all performed out of the men’s overwhelming joy.
In Lumbinī, the sprout of a Buddha was born, welcomed for the welfare of humanity. || 8 ||
Having drunk [the nectar], people attain satisfaction; likewise, the trees, with eyes devoid of blinking under the guise of flowers, seem to behold the nectar of his true form with their own eyes.
To delight him, the sky instantly spreads a beautiful canopy of clouds.
With joy, the earth trembles again and again, performing a festival of swings. || 9 ||
He produces supreme joy for Māyā and glory for Śuddhodana; he elevates the lineage and community of the Śākyas; he becomes the refuge for men in the world;
he accomplishes great benefit and happiness for sentient beings; and he brings peace to the wrong views of men.
Homage to you, the Protector, who uplifts the worlds through great compassion. 10.
Thus ends the first section, titled "The Auspicious Birth," in the poem *Śrī Buddhodaya* composed by the monk-scholar Śānti.
The second episode:
the arrival of Asita,
heard from ear to ear throughout the land at the outset, in the illustrious Lumbinī grove.
Subsequently, when the Lord Śuddhodana resided in the city known as Śrīkapilāvastu,
the account of the conduct of the Sugata’s sprout— from the Himālaya mountains to the Vindhya range, through the divine abodes of virtuous celestial rishis— began to circulate among the people. (11)
Indeed, when he hears from a person a delightful tale concerning the Bodhisattvas, he adorns it and recounts it to another with joy and a clear heart;
thus, for one whose form is the very essence of auspiciousness, his birth is clearly a blessing for all the worlds.
In this matter, every person, though bowed with devotion, became uplifted; thus did all the people perceive. ||12||
Having heard of his existence as the pacifier of the suffering of worldly existence and the treasury of all auspiciousness;
considering the incomparable good fortune of Bhāratavarṣa to have been adorned by his birth;
and perceiving that this entire circle of the earth has become free from affliction through his appearance—
Though free from desire, the sage Asita went to that best of children, wishing to see him.
Having honored that best of sages with devotion, King Śuddhodana respectfully offered himself, along with his entire kingdom and kinsmen, to him, saying:
"Having shown me compassion, what dear service may I perform for you now that you have arrived here?"
"O Great Sage, instruct your disciple quickly," he said, joining his palms in reverence.

I have no need for wealth, nor any interest in the king; I have no need for sovereignty, nor any interest in houses. I am joyful having abandoned my home for the forest solitude. Whatever people and wealth were offered to me today, O sir, let all that remain yours alone.
It is my desire to behold your son; oh, fulfill that wish alone! 15.
Likewise, observing the heart of the eminent sage to be supremely delighted with his own son, the king, bowed down by a weight of joy, fulfilled the sage’s desire; he placed his own son,
who was resplendent in the lap of the nurse and possessed a face as beautiful as the full moon, [before him].
Out of affection, he brought that which was enchanting to the world before the best of sages.

To the assembly, [I offer praise] to the excellent child who is enchanting to the world and its beyond, who bestows the accomplishment of all aims, who is perfect with a wealth of auspicious marks, who bears the vastness of the glory of his form,
and who is the very seed of the great tree of the Tathāgata, visibly sprouted within the multitude.
Having observed the Śākyas and the Śākya king, the Brahmanical seer spoke thus: || 17 ||
May the great being, the Sage Asita, perceive the supremely beautiful tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which curls to the right;
may he behold this dance of the glory of the Dharma.
Behold the prince, the sprout of the Sugatas, exceedingly delicate and marked by the [major] characteristics. (a)
Let it be understood that his two very broad arms, though appearing as mere children hanging down to his knees, are superhuman and not infantile, and are capable of protecting this entire universe.
Behold the prince, the sprout of the Sugatas, most delicate and marked with the primary characteristics! Āḥ!
May this one, whose hands and feet are marked with webbing, awaken from his slumber after crushing Māra;
surely he will become the refuge here for all living beings.
Behold the prince, the sprout of the Sugatas, most delicate and marked with the primary characteristics. ||i||
Behold his two most beautiful feet, adorned with wheels;
truly, both of them shall become self-controlled gods among men in this world.
Behold the prince, the sprout of the Sugatas, exceedingly delicate and marked by the primary characteristics. ||ī||
May he understand the treasury protected by shame to be like a treasury of elephant-treasure;
may even the daughters of Māra long to pay homage to him who is free from fault.
Behold the prince, the scion of the Sugatas, most delicate and marked with the primary characteristics! ||u||
May he manifest a smile upon his serene and noble face—
a smile that inspires wonder and pacifies the darkness of the eyes of all people, like the rising of the sun.
Behold the prince, the sprout of the Sugatas, exceedingly delicate and marked with the primary characteristics. ||ū||
May his face, though currently devoid of speech, now inspire satisfaction;
for the progenitor of the Teacher of the World will surely bring about the true contentment of the world.
Behold the prince, the scion of the Sugatas, most delicate and marked with the primary characteristics. ||Ṛ||
May the world behold with its very eyes this child who is no child, the destroyer of dualities;
through him, the world shall surely attain the path free from the web of the Kali age.
Behold the prince, the sprout of the Sugatas, most delicate and marked with the primary characteristics. ||Ṛ||
Gazing with supreme reverence at that son of Śuddhodana, the Sage uttered a beautiful song and brought satisfaction to the King of the Śākyas through his prophecies;
yet behold, something else arose in the mind of the Brahman-sage in an instant.
With his eyes filled with tears directed toward the sky, he became choked in his throat. || 18 ||
Seeing that deity of the earth standing thus with a faltering voice, his mind overwhelmed by grief at that moment, his eyes filled with tears,
the lord of the earth became afraid, his heart full of doubt regarding the prince.
Placing his joined palms in supplication upon his head, he spoke these words to the distressed woman.
The king [perceived] the joy of all his kinsmen, the entire community, and the people of the city and the kingdom,
as well as the manifold excellence proclaimed by the Brahmins who were experts in the annual rites for the gods.
Having spoken thus of this one who has arisen for the benefit of the entire world, why do you weep with such dejection? (a)
It was attended by the dancing of throngs of men and women and groups of boys and girls,
and honored by various kinds of musical performances arising from the songs of sweet-voiced birds.
Having spoken thus of this [Buddha] who has arisen for the benefit of the entire world, why do you weep so sorrowfully? Āḥ!
His body was adorned with the certainty of being a Great Being, as indicated by his marks;
he was destined to attain enlightenment, free from the stains of strife and the delusion of doubt.
Having spoken thus of this one who has arisen for the welfare of the entire world, why do you weep with such dejection? ||i||
It is the treasury of peace that shakes off passion and hatred and uproots violence;
it is the primary cause for becoming worthy of worship by all the virtuous people in the world.
Having spoken thus of this one who has arisen for the welfare of the entire world, why do you weep so sorrowfully? || 10 ||
The abundance of all grains, wealth, happiness,
and prosperity beneficial to one's own birth is equal to the mass of one's own most supremely enchanting form.
Having spoken thus of this one who has arisen for the welfare of the entire world, why do you weep with such dejection? ||u||
Its news was known by the multitudes of people throughout the cities, districts, and provinces;
it was exceedingly beautiful, like a most beloved one who has newly attained the rising of a medicinal herb.
Having spoken of this which has arisen for the benefit of the entire world, why do you weep with such dejection? (U)
He who removes the suffering of all people submerged in the pain of being repeatedly plundered and oppressed;
he who is the supreme refuge for those without shelter and the sole abode of bliss.
Having spoken thus of this one who has arisen for the welfare of the entire world, why do you weep with such sorrow? (Ṛ)
In this world, the Tathāgata has proclaimed his various and peerless state,
having become a supreme savior by bestowing upon the worlds a rain consisting of the nectar of immortality.
Having spoken thus of this one who has arisen for the welfare of the entire world, why do you weep with such dejection? ||Ṛ||
The sage Asita, wearing a saffron robe, makes his heart free from all passions;
with a rain of the nectar of Dharma, he extinguishes the fire of afflictions and the suffering of rebirth.
"I shall not hear the Hero speaking;
thus I weep. Alas, it is my time to depart, leaving this body behind. ||a||
He is being praised as incomparable by all the worlds, who bestows great honor;
he is worthy of reverence here even by those of great pride, yet he himself is free from arrogance.
"I shall not hear the Hero speaking"—thus I weep; alas, it is my time to depart, leaving this body behind. || Ā ||
A single family, a unique family of the Dharma, producing new beings among the people,
and bringing to rest the entire multitude of human lineages— both high and low, noble and base.
"I shall not hear the Hero speaking;
thus I weep. Alas, it is my time to depart, leaving this body behind. ii.
From the summit of Mount Sumeru to the furthest limit of Mount Kumeru,
between the mountains of sunrise and sunset, it unifies all these people.
"I shall not hear the Hero speaking"—"I shall hear the Hero speaking"—thus I weep; alas, let my time to depart come, leaving this body behind. ||ī||
He who leads people by means of the Dharma along the incomparable path to prosperity,
and who fashions this human being with virtues worthy of worship by gods and men.
"I shall not hear the Hero speaking;
thus I weep. Alas, it is my time to depart, leaving this body behind. ||u||
He who, by the flood of compassion, completely extinguishes the intense fire of violence,
and by loving-kindness, sets aside all talk of slaughter, imprisonment, and violent warfare.
"I shall not hear the Hero speaking," thus I weep; alas, it is my time to depart, leaving this body behind. ||ū||

I shall not hear the Hero speaking— he who, by his own wisdom, cuts asunder the diverse web of conflicting doctrines, and who, having taught the universal empire consisting of the Dharma, shatters the age of strife (kali).
Thus I weep; alas, the time has come for me to depart, leaving this body behind. ||Ṛ||
To this Buddha, the crusher of Māra and the son of King Śākya, who was honored by all men, kings, and the wives of kings;
"I shall not hear the Hero speak"—thus I weep; alas, it is my time to depart, leaving this body behind. ||ṝ||
"O King, seeing me weeping thus, do not be despondent;
whatever I have said will all certainly come to pass.
Having spoken thus and bestowed auspicious blessings upon the Śākya king, [he departed].
The Brahmin, honored by all people, went from the royal palace to his own hermitage. ||20||
Thus ends the second episode, titled "The Arrival of Asita," in the poem *Śrī Buddhodaya* composed by the monk-scholar Śānti.
The third episode:
the acceptance of the cowherds,
by which he brought about his own rise after his father had been intent on the non-arising of all prosperity.

In this place, Siddhārtha, increasing day by day along with his own growth in years, gladdened his family with childhood sports during the moments of infancy; then, having entered the stage of youth, the wise youth, having quickly mastered the sciences under a teacher, shone forth. (21)
Seeing that youth had arisen in his own son— a sight so desirable for maidens— the king set his mind upon choosing an excellent bride from among the Gaṇas,
desiring to learn from the mouths of the prince’s friends their disposition toward her.
The leader of the Śākya clan received these new words from his own son.
O Prince, she who would be delightful by her beauty and gladden the heart with her virtues,
she who would find pleasure only in me and think of nothing external, such as wealth or land; [let her be given to me].
I would choose a maiden, my lovely and delicate companion, who is my sole helper in the practice of dharma. (a)
Even when born into a great family, one should have no pride;
even when born into a lowly family, one should certainly have no contempt.
I would choose a maiden—my sole companion in the practice of dharma, lovely and delicate. ||ā||
That virtuous woman who does not take pride in her birth during a wedding or a marriage— she,
possessing a mind characterized by good conduct, understands that virtues come and go, whereas birth remains constant.
I would choose such a maiden—a lovely and delicate girl who is my sole companion in the practice of dharma. ||i||
She who, when her husband is away on a journey, never directs her thoughts toward another man;
she who does not commit infidelity even when deprived of wealth due to misfortune.
I would choose such a maiden as my sole companion in the practice of dharma—one who is lovely, delicate, and virtuous. ||ī||
I would choose a maiden who always treats her mother-in-law as a mother, who is not intoxicated even by her own good fortune,
who treats her father-in-law as a father, and who is skilled in the duties of the family and ever vigilant.
Her, who was the sole companion in the practice of dharma, lovely and delicate— ||| u |||
She who is skilled in the arts, whose mind is not fickle toward a granary,
who has virtue alone as her ornament, and who is not enamored by ornaments of gems and gold.
I would choose that maiden, my lovely and delicate companion in the sole practice of dharma. ||ū||
The fortunate girl who drinks and eats in moderation, who is habituated to measured expenditure,
who guards the household goods, and protects the family, is truly blessed.
I would choose a maiden, my sole companion in the practice of dharma, lovely and delicate. ||Ṛ||
What need is there for much? She should assist her husband and show compassion even toward other people;
she should always act with a beneficial intent and cultivate virtue within her mind.
I would choose a maiden—my sole companion in the practice of dharma, lovely and delicate. ||Ṛ||
Thus, having understood the desire of his son's heart, the Lord of the Śākyas quickly commanded the twice-born to search for a maiden endowed with every excellence.
Having heard from them that his younger sister Daṇḍapāṇi was to be given in marriage to one worthy of her son,
he held a festival to celebrate the union of Siddhārtha’s eyes with her.
While the prince was distracted at that festival by the various gifts being offered by the maidens with sidelong glances cast from their eyes,
Gopā approached him at that very moment, smiling, as he was occupied with the distribution of the vessels.
At that very moment, he gave the ring together with his heart.

Knowing that his son Gopa was deeply attached [to her], and having been requested by the son’s teacher, he— though desirous of giving his daughter to that very man, the best of heroes— did not do so; therefore,
in order to protect his own reputation, he likewise took Gopa [as a hostage].
In order to display his skill, he commanded the king to make a public proclamation among the assembly.
Having made Yaśodharā alone the banner of victory for the Śākyas in the world, the illustrious Bodhisattva shone forth, having overcome all [others] before them;
seeing that, the proud and great [king] took his own daughter with his own hand.
Śrī Daṇḍapāṇi bestowed [the gift] upon King Siddhārtha and brought him great joy.
That cowherd girl, though living openly in her father-in-law’s house just as she had in her father’s home, conducted herself before the elders without a veil;
through her friendliness toward the assembly of people, she brought joy to the hearts of all.
She spoke of them as a mere trifle to those who consider only deep-rooted attachment to be of great value in their hearts.
Gopā, who is not ashamed of herself, who fears nothing in this world out of modesty,
who is never clothed in truth, is indeed equal to one who is naked.
What is the use of her face being covered by a cloth, or of that wealth of intellect which is but two finger-breadths deep?
She who was solely occupied with her own adornment while in the kitchen—was she not born so as to know what exists outside the world? Her mind was not directed toward that.
What is the use of her face being covered by a cloth, she whose wealth of intellect consists of only two fingers? Alas!
She who knows the mortar and the basin, she who knows the grinding stone and the millstone,
and she who knows her own servitude— what fruit remains in this world for such folly?
What is the use of her face being covered by a cloth, when her wealth of intelligence consists of only two fingers? (i)
That knowledge which grinds within the house along with one's own self,
and which knows that there is no happiness here without it— [that alone is true knowledge].
What is the use of her face being covered by a cloth, she whose wealth of intellect consists of only two fingers? (II)
One fills a water-pot with its own liquid, not with life;
there is no scripture or craft whatsoever that can sew up a wound.
What is the use of her face being covered by a cloth, she whose wealth of intelligence consists of only two fingers? 11.30u.
She who is the ruin of her family, whose only fruit is indeed suffering,
and whose beauty is her sole strength— yet that strength is but momentary stability.
What is the use of her face being covered by a cloth, when her wealth of intellect consists of only two fingers? ||ū||
Through craving, one becomes excessively attached to houses and the accumulation of wealth and grain;
yet she who does not think of anything here, being free from passion, possesses merit in this world.
What is the use of that woman who covers her face with a cloth, she whose wealth of intellect is but two finger-breadths? ||Ṛ||
She who is not as bold as a man, she who does not possess the wisdom of a man,
she who lacks the heroic spirit of a man, and she whose livelihood is not like that of a man.
What is the use of her face being covered by a cloth, she whose wealth of intellect consists of only two fingers? ||ṝ||

Having thus recognized Yaśodharā as preeminent in beauty and virtues, and as one whose character was well-restrained within herself yet fully revealed in her role as a leader among her group, the king—
out of affection, like a father rejoicing in his own daughter— covered her with garments and jewels.
Accompanied by words of benediction, she joyfully sang these auspicious verses.
Śuddhodana always shines with beauty through his open face, as if with a flower.
We are greatly blessed by you;
you have revealed yourself as a virtuous maiden. ||a||
Just as a jewel, so too does one's worth become manifest through a face that is always open.
We are greatly blessed by you;
you have revealed yourself as a virtuous maiden. || Ā ||
Why does it shine with such radiance within, as if its mouth were always open?
We are most fortunate by you;
you, O Sukanyā, have revealed yourself. ii.
For just as with a mirror,
so too does one's inner state always bear fruit through the face.
We are greatly blessed by you;
you have revealed yourself as a virtuous maiden. ||ī||
Everyone is satisfied by a face that is open when hearing pleasant words.
We are greatly blessed by you;
you have revealed yourself as a virtuous maiden. ||u||
The teacher here rejoices with a face adorned by modesty, as it were,
revealed.
We are most fortunate by you;
you, Sukanyā, have revealed yourself. || ū ||
One should remain concealed regarding one's faults;
one should be open regarding one's virtues.
We are greatly blessed by you;
you have revealed yourself as a virtuous maiden. ||Ṛ||
You are endowed with beauty and virtue;
your splendor is revealed by your countenance.
We are most fortunate because of you.
You, O Sukanyā, have been revealed. ||Ṛ||
Thus he addressed that cowherd woman, who was supremely devoted to her own son, who was entirely intent on devotion toward her elders and possessed supreme friendliness toward all other people,
and who was gladdened by blessings for the abundance of good fortune accompanied by happiness.
Having smelled the crown of his bowed head, the Lord of the Śākyas rejoiced among the Śākyas.
Just as that Blessed One was endowed with all virtues— the sprout from the seed of the illustrious Buddha—
so too was that Blessed Lady endowed with all virtues, her mind thick with compassion;
a brilliant mutual companionship arose between those two youths.
Seeing that, the minds of both Rati and Kāma also became filled with longing.
Thus ends the third episode, titled "The Acceptance of Gopā," in the poem *Śrī Buddhodaya* composed by the monk-scholar Śānti.
The fourth episode:
Having obtained Gopā as his consort through the sight of the sign, that virtuous one attained renown among the assembly.
He joyfully rendered manifold assistance to his father’s faction in their various undertakings;

yet, seeing that the factions were intent on mutual injury, devoted solely to their own interests, and possessed weapons as their highest goal, he was not pleased— even though they were his own kinsmen— seeing them divided within his own home.
The moment of bliss is indeed most difficult for a householder to find in this world; alas, for one devoted to strife, life passes away day and night almost entirely in vain.
The warrior lives only for evil, having slain his own kin and others with weapons.
May the world be free from enmity; what path is there for people here to attain the necessary conditions? 32.
Reflecting thus, he became despondent while confined within his home; seeing that his mind was deeply distressed, he resolved to go outside the city to the forest to soothe his heart.
Mounted upon a chariot, his slender body was clearly seen by the women.
The prince was gazed upon with joy by the citizens, who were intent on shouts of victory. ||33||

On the road, where the water had been sprinkled and the dust was cleared away, which was crowded with people and made charming through the efforts of men intent on royal commands— even though it was devoid of objects that inspire spiritual urgency and was filled only with sounds of worldly joy—
Seeing an old man, he asked his charioteer with curiosity, "Who is this? ||34||
Regarding the prince, this charioteer was also formerly a skilled warrior who, having donned firm armor,
was victorious in battle.
Now he is utterly despised;
now his body is consumed by old age. ||a||
In former times, he too was endowed with beauty and strength; his limbs were well-anointed with unguents, and he wore a forest garland.
Now he is utterly despised;
now his body is consumed by old age. || Ā ||
In former times, upon seeing him, the city women were deeply attached to him and became intoxicated with passion.
Now he is utterly despised;
now his body is consumed by old age. ||i||
Having heard his words previously, those endowed with virtue said, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Now he is utterly despised;
now his body is consumed by old age. || 1 ||
He too, in former times, supported his kinsmen and attained great renown in the world.
Now he is utterly despised;
now his body is consumed by old age. ||u||
By him, wealth was previously acquired here,
and the hearts of all people were won over.
Now he is utterly despised;
now his body is consumed by old age. || Ū ||
In former times, he possessed beauty, strength, wealth, intelligence, and knowledge, as well as great self-esteem.
Now he is utterly despised;
now his body is consumed by old age. || Ṛ ||
This destiny shall befall everyone:
formerly the earth was under his power,
but now he has been utterly humiliated.
Now his body is licked by old age. (Ṛ)

Distressed by old age, the prince turned back from his journey and returned to his own home; yet there he was again obstructed, for the king’s son desired to go forth once more to the forest for pleasure. Seeing on the very street of the city a man afflicted by disease and suffering, he himself became deeply moved.
When asked, "Who is he?", Yantra explained everything in detail.
Regarding the prince, the charioteer reflects: "His body suffers, his mind falls into agitation,
and he experiences pain where there was previously ease."
"Deprived here indeed of enjoyments,
he now languishes because of illness."
He breathes heavily due to wind and finds no relief;
neither food nor drink brings him any pleasure.
Indeed, he has been cheated of enjoyments here;
he now languishes because of disease. ||ā||
Even while seeing the worlds, he sees nothing at all;
his vision is empty, and not even the slightest object of sight manifests for him.
Indeed, he is cheated here of enjoyments;
he suffers from disease. (8)
Trembling seizes his body and his mind abandons its fortitude;
unable to stand still, he cannot even hold his neck steady.
Indeed, deceived here by sensual pleasures, he now languishes because of disease. ||1||
Piteously crying out in agony with a tearful face, he said: "O Mother! Alas, Father, O King! Protect me, protect me! Alas, alas!"
Deprived here indeed of enjoyments, he truly languishes because of disease. || u ||
Life exists within the body, yet there is no well-being for it;
there is only suffering, only suffering, and only suffering.
Indeed, he is deprived of enjoyments here;
he suffers from disease. ||ū||
When the humors, elements, and waste products in his body become disturbed,
he approaches a physician to obtain the medicine for that purpose.
Deprived here indeed of enjoyments, he truly languishes because of disease. ||Ṛ||
When the entire collection of humors is agitated, this is the condition for everyone;
and for this [individual], the collection of humors is agitated, having cast aside equilibrium.
Deprived here indeed of enjoyments, he truly languishes because of disease. (Ṛ)
Seeing people overwhelmed by intense pain and afflicted, he— though naturally healthy— became deeply moved and regarded his own body as if it were long-suffering and ill;
turning back from his departure, the sprout of the seed of the Blessed Buddha returned home.
Even though he had attained perfect happiness, he experienced incomparable suffering intensely within his mind.
Extremely distressed by a sense of spiritual urgency, he beheld the world within his own heart as being subject to the constraints of time;
seeing the age of Kali prevailing among the worlds, the self-possessed one remained constantly with a weary heart,
not attaining even a fragment of happiness within his inner apartments.
Having seen the forest from the city, he went forth to delight his own heart.
But as the person was being carried out, motionless yet adorned, along the very street crowded with others wailing piteously, the prince’s gaze fell upon him;
and when asked by the son of the king, "Who is this?", the charioteer spoke at length.
Beholding him thus distraught in mind, he spoke these words to increase his sense of spiritual urgency.
O charioteer,
every person born here perishes;
in the end, no one at all beholds them.
The measure of one's lifespan is filled;
such is the end that occurs for everyone in this world. ||a||
One eats, drinks, sleeps, and awakens;
yet in the end, departure is accomplished here,
and the measure of one's lifespan is fulfilled.
Such is the end that comes to everyone in this world. || Ā ||
He plays, laughs, and attends upon his wife;
yet he departs from the world for the ultimate end.
The measure of one’s lifespan is fulfilled;
for everyone in this world, such is the final end. ||i||
He acquires wealth, protects it, and experiences happiness;
at the end he passes away, and hereafter he does not come into existence again.
The measure of one's lifespan is fulfilled;
such is the end that occurs for everyone in this world. ||ī||
He fights, he conquers, he sacrifices, and he attains happiness;
in the end, however, he returns to non-existence.
The measure of one's lifespan is fulfilled;
for everyone in this world, such is the final end. ||u||
From somewhere it is born; to somewhere it goes. No one protects that which departs from the world.
The span of life is fulfilled;
such is the end that occurs for everyone in this world. ||ū||
No one at all wanders upon this earth who is free from old age;
no one at all sports here on this earth who is immortal.
The measure of one’s lifespan is fulfilled;
such is the end that occurs for everyone in this world. ||ṛ||
When the fire has departed from the body,
people honor another person in this very same way.
The span of life is fulfilled;
for everyone in this world, such is the end. ||Ṛ||

In the past, even though he was filled with agitation upon beholding the world— intent on mutual injury, perpetually devoted to such conduct, fallen from the totality of virtues due to the impurities of the Kali age,
surrounded by hosts consisting of passion and hatred, devoid of compassion, and deceitful— [he remained steadfast].
Having gazed at her, who remained for only a moment, he now looked intently at Uḍava.
Is strife alone the life of the world, or is unity conceivable anywhere?
Is violence here indeed the law, or is there also a sense of compassion among people?
This world is worn out and intent on death; that which is called youth is but illusion.
Having contemplated that all this is empty, he returned once again to his very home.
Thus ends the fourth section, titled "The Vision of Omens," in the poem *Śrī-Buddhodaya* composed by the monk-scholar Śānti.
The fifth section:
The Forest Retreat,
in which the desire cherished by the Śākya clan at the moment of his birth was fulfilled.
First it sprouted; then, when the best of youths reached adolescence, it grew with leaves;
and now that he has attained fresh manhood, it has fully blossomed—O, why does this tree not now burst forth with excellent fruits? (41)

Having abandoned the giving of gifts and the conquest of the earth, having turned away from worldly attachment, he will not go to the station of a universal monarch; for what [use] is that which grants all worldly success? Having renounced the Śākya clan, forsaken the king, as well as his wife Gautamī—
Having gone to the forest, will he become one devoted to the practice of begging among the people? ||42||

As the king and his retinue were thus occupied day and night with such anxieties— while they were generally preoccupied with the enjoyment of sensual pleasures through women— the king, desiring to attain peace of mind, departed from the city by means of a mechanical vehicle.
By the king's command, Śrīghana went to see the forest frequented by birds and deer.
Seeing there an ascetic with serene faculties, free from anxiety and devoid of worldly attachment, the prince inquired, "Who is this? and received the reply, "This one is devoted to the Dharma.
Approaching that tranquil man with humble words, the prince questioned him.
By what means, O Blessed One, do you dwell so exceedingly unafflicted among the afflicted and happy among those who suffer? (44)
Having heard these words, the ascetic— recognizing him as the best among men in this world who possess self-restraint, the supreme savior of the universe, and the destroyer of the pride of Kandarpa—
and seeing that the world was established in such a state, both harsh and yet exultant with passion;
To him, who was deeply agitated and yet striving for supreme peace within his heart as he attained tranquility, he spoke: || 45 ||
I am an ascetic without a fixed abode; alms are very easy for me to obtain, and I dwell at ease.
I am not bound by anyone or anything; I wander according to my own will.
Now the mind is free from bondage; now it is liberated through the absence of longing for the lady Vasu. (a)
In this world, people engage in cattle-rearing and slaughter animals for sacrifice;
I have no need here for such cattle, but rather rice and barley for the sake of dharma.
"Now the mind is free from bondage; now it is liberated through the absence of longing for the lady Vasu. ||a||
The world rears cows, goats, and sheep for food only to slaughter them;
yet here, it is possible to pass even another day by subsisting on vegetables alone.
Now the mind is free from bondage; now it is liberated through the absence of longing for the lady of wealth. ||i||
A man kills another man; he thinks, "This battle is for the sake of dharma.
But I have realized that in this world there is not even a trace of dharma in violence.
Now the mind is free from bondage; now it is liberated through the absence of longing for the lady of wealth. ||ī||
In this world, a pair [of opposites] indeed exists under the pretext of dharma for the sake of enjoyment;
yet a pair of garments together with a mere measure of food is truly sufficient for the needs of the body.
Now the mind is free from bondage; now it is liberated through the absence of longing for the lady of wealth. ||u||
A single bed is sufficient even for a king for the sake of sleep;
yet the ascetic sleeps happily upon a layer of grass for the sake of preserving his happiness.
Now the mind is free from bondage; now it is liberated through the absence of longing for the lady of wealth. ||ū||
Food, clothing, bedding, and shelter are desired by everyone here;
however, when wealth is focused on even one of these, it produces everything undesirable.
Now the mind is free from bondage; now it is liberated by the absence of longing for the lady of wealth. ||ṛ||
The entire wealth of women on earth is not sufficient for even a single person;
and without a delight in sharing, the mind never attains peace.
Now the mind is free from bondage; now it is liberated through the absence of longing for the splendors of wealth. ||Ṛ||
Having heard the words of the holy man, which were directed toward renunciation and endowed with tranquility,
his mind— which had previously been distressed by attachment to the forest— became somewhat composed. Having reflected upon that matter for a long time, he eventually departed from that grove.
On the road, the prince heard a maiden singing—the emaciated daughter of Gautama.
Emaciated Gautami’s body experiences an unprecedented and entirely different thrill, with every hair standing on end;
meanwhile, an extraordinary tranquility awakens intensely within my own restless mind.
She has found her peace here;
for one who possesses such a beloved, the ordainer of fortune is truly desirable. ||a||
Evil intention departs from the heart, and wholesome intention enters the heart;
a certain pure mental state, imbued with affection, arises.
She is blessed here, for her beloved is so desirable that the ordainer of fortune has been kind to her. ||a||
The eyes, filled with joy, laugh; the noble face laughs;
and the inner heart laughs, chuckles, and laughs aloud again and again.
That beloved woman has found peace here, for whose sake such a desirable lover has been ordained by the dispensation of fortune. ||i||
Joy throbs in her chest; joy radiates steadily within her mind;
her body experiences some indescribable, unprecedented happiness never before felt.
Here, that beloved woman has found perfect bliss.
He whose beloved is such as this is one whose destiny has been ordained by a most desirable fate. ||ī||
The senses are joyful; many [virtues] have arisen from past good deeds.
Oh, how blessed, how blessed is this day! How fruitful are my body and eyes!
She is blessed here, for her beloved is such that the ordainer of fortune has made him so desirable. ||u||
Indeed, it is only the pair of eyes that constitutes her body; her form is not composed of eyes alone.
Yet, through the mere sight of her, delight arises, and the restless heart finds no satiety.
That beloved woman has found her rest here, for whose sake such a desirable lover and ordainer of fortune has been created. ||ū||
These two hands have gone again and again to salute the head;
the head bows once, twice, thrice, and many times in order to show honor.
She is blessed here, for her beloved is so desirable that the ordainer of fortune has been kind to her. ||ṛ||
In this matter, that father has surely attained peace, and that mother has certainly found rest,
from whose own limbs this son was born to bring them joy.
She is blessed here with such a beloved, for one whose fortune-dispenser has made him so desirable. ||Ṛ||
Having heard from the mouth of the maiden that he had attained the supreme state of Nirvana, he sent her a pearl necklace as a gift— a favorite of his own that was no longer worn.
Then, having returned home, he was neither dejected nor elated, remaining just as he had been before.
Maintaining composure in his mind, the valiant one went to the king and spoke.
When the prince returns for a moment and you are no longer here in this world, O father,
I too shall no longer exist; tell me, O lord of men, what will you do with me?
My mind finds no delight;
seeing that this is impermanent, unstable, and empty, it attains detachment.
"This body is not ageless; it is ever-afflicted and fragile as a moment.
Having beheld the world defiled by the impurity of the Kali age, my mind has become restless."
My mind finds no delight;
seeing that this is impermanent, unstable, and empty, it attains detachment. ||a||
If today there is no separation, or if tomorrow it shall come under the power of death,
then enough, my dear, with this sensual bait that is like the taste of wine— a thing that lasts but a moment.
My mind finds no delight;
seeing that this is impermanent, unstable, and empty, it attains detachment. ||i||
Disease will lead him to the abode of Yama, or his body will perish in battle;
alas, he shall obtain nothing in this world, and no one here is his companion.
My mind finds no delight;
seeing that this is impermanent, unstable, and empty, it attains detachment. ||8||
This youth will pass away quickly, and I shall become devoid of strength;
O father, what shall I do then when I am overcome by old age and miserable?
My mind finds no delight;
seeing that this is impermanent, unstable, and empty, it attains detachment. ||u||
What discourse on dharma and artha can there be when the body is no longer capable even of breathing?
This is my time for dharma and artha; I shall now fulfill the purpose of my own mind.
My mind finds no delight;
seeing that this is impermanent, unstable, and empty, it attains detachment. ||ū||
Indeed, I have no need for wealth that is acquired over many kalpas and is intent on violence;
my own interest is the Dharma centered on tranquility, for I desire peace and seek the goal of peace.
My mind finds no delight;
seeing that this is impermanent, unstable, and empty, it attains detachment. ||ṛ||
This mind desires to go forth as a wanderer for the sake of the Dharma, to enter the forest of asceticism;
grant me permission to practice the Dharma in order to conquer the armies of the passions.
The mind finds no delight in me;
seeing that this is impermanent, unstable, and empty, it attains detachment. ||ṛ||
Having heard the words of Siddhārtha, the king, his eyes filled with tears,
observed the prince’s firm resolve toward the Dharma and contemplated the suffering in the forest; yet,
his heart overflowing with affection for his son and worldly attachment, he intended to restrain his son at home.
He spoke words endowed with the meaning of the Vedas for the sake of detachment and peace.
What you have said here is all true; indeed, nothing in this world is eternal.
Nevertheless, one must certainly perform what is appropriate and was honored by one's ancestors:
study during childhood, and then, when one has reached youth, the taking of a wife.
In the householder stage, however, one should follow the conduct of one's lineage for the sake of dharma; at the end, one should practice austerity.
This is not the time for you to go to the forest; this age is fraught with faults, and it is censurable for one worthy of enjoyment to abandon the home and turn back from the woods.
Do not go now; a long time remains for you here to perform ascetic penance.
Having thus instructed him, the king said: "Go home and rejoice."
Thus ends the fifth episode, titled "The Forest Retreat," in the poem *Śrī Buddhodaya* composed by Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī.
The sixth section: Departure.
I contemplate deeply in my heart whatever is appropriate for the illusory display.
No one in the royal court gazes upon him even for a moment, not even in a dream;

and the king himself, turned away from the path of cessation and always delighting in worldly activity, treats me as if I were a mere child, commanding me through a long succession of playful diversions. (51)
Thus, having performed all the duties appropriate for the end of the day— intent upon such reflections in his heart— and then having found the opportunity,
he ascended a beautiful celestial chariot resounding with the sounds of conchs, songs, and musical instruments.
The beautiful women, with their lovely faces and smiling eyes, sang to delight him.
O fair-eyed one, while you are present, this dwelling shines forth and puts even the abode of the gods to shame;
wherever you sport here, even that forest becomes a city that subdues pride.
O you who possess a golden-hued body that crushes passion and pride,
you who dwell in the garden of the heart familiar with the supportless bliss— be victorious!
Though this house is crowded with many people, it appears utterly empty;
at the mere sight of you not being present for even a moment, my heart succumbs to the pangs of separation.
You bear a golden-hued body that crushes the pride of the God of Love.
Victory to you, who dwell in the garden of the heart, familiar with the bliss of the supportless! Āḥ!
You are life, you alone are the vital breath; we long for nothing but you. Always take delight with us, so that we may serve you alone.
O you who possess a body as golden-hued as it crushes passion and pride, you who sport in the garden of the heart familiar with the supportless bliss—be victorious! ||i||
When you go outside, these parrots and these mynas cry out incessantly, "Where is the prince? until you have returned.
O you who possess a body as golden-hued as the crusher of passion and pride, you who dwell in the garden of the heart familiar with the supportless bliss—be victorious! ||ī||
They do not obtain their eyes even for the blink of an eyelash by their own will;
rather, the opening and closing of those two occur only by chance.
O you who possess a body as golden-hued as it crushes passion and pride;
victory to you, who dwell in the garden of the heart familiar with supportless bliss! (u)
People say that you have gone to the forest to dispel your mental distress;
but are there not creepers, branches, birds, deer, and the like in the pleasure grove?
O you who possess a body as golden-hued as gold that crushes passion and pride;
victory to you, who sport in the garden of a heart familiar with the supportless bliss! ||ū||
If you go outside, we too must be led back at that very time;
one must not depart otherwise, for we must remain here constantly.
O you who possess a body as golden-hued as it crushes passion and pride;
may you be victorious, you whose heart delights in dwelling within the garden of the supportless bliss! (Ṛ)
Our very lives always abide in you alone; you are our dearest.
That you go out alone is the decree of fate; it is not a good thing.
O you who possess a golden-hued body that crushes passion and pride, victory to you who dwell in the garden of the heart, which is familiar with the bliss of the supportless! ||ṝ||

Having heard these words spoken by the Śākya women, which were moist with the weight of affection, the prince— his mind tender with love and his thoughts compassionate— became somewhat despondent; yet,
being intent on the forest, he did not wish to abandon his own people because of their harshness.
But rather, he constantly directs his great mind toward attaining that which is truly great. || 53 ||

The women, with their graceful limbs, drew the minds of even the insentient toward this most delicate couch upon which he sat, by means of dances accompanied by gestures, and by the sweet singing of verses to the accompaniment of musical instruments— all performed with an abundance of compassionate feeling.
Out of friendship, they provided entertainment for his mind through various appropriate modes of hospitality. (54)
Though turned away from the musical concert, that youth, intent on thought within his heart,
fell into a yogic sleep even as those lovely-eyed women were dancing;
when he had fallen asleep, the entire inner apartment, though rich in splendor, was as if fast asleep.
But in the body there is much that is loathsome; that which he perceived while awake was this. ||55||

Having awakened and seen them, those women with beautiful garments were cast into the cremation ground; through their contortions, they fell into a state of transformation, performing the antics of female ghosts to the one who bestows suffering.
Then, seeing his daughter and the cowherd woman lying there, he departed for the forest.
At night, accompanied only by his horse Kanthaka and his groom Chandaka, he departed from the city.
Having attained the lowest state at the time of dawn, he went forth at sunrise; thereafter,
intending to traverse the earth in every direction with his footprints as a mark,
he resolved to turn back his horse and chariot to deliver his own message.
The wise and new sage spoke to the steadfast man, who was full of affection for his people. ||57||
O best of sages,
it was not out of a heart devoid of affection that I did not abandon my home; rather, there was nothing there that I desired, and for that reason I left.
I go for refuge to that supreme Dharma, wherein there is no mutual deception, in order to pursue it. (a)
I wish to see people who possess true wealth and are virtuous;
I consider a place devoid of wicked people to be the highest state, even if it is uninhabited.
I go for refuge to that supreme Dharma, wherein there is no mutual deception, in order to pursue it. ||a||
I wish to hear words that are true and pleasant;
I do not wish to follow crookedness at all.
I go for refuge indeed to that supreme Dharma, wherein there is no mutual deception, in order to pursue it. ||i||
Wherever indeed war, slaughter, or imprisonment exists,
there evil intent increases through violence.
I go for refuge indeed to that supreme Dharma, wherein there is no mutual deception, and which one should pursue. ||ī||
Neither is one a Brahmin by birth, nor is one a Śūdra;
if Brahminhood is desired here, it is attained through action.
I go for refuge to that supreme Dharma, in which there is no mutual deception, in order to pursue it. ||u||
Let them conduct themselves with compassion; let them proceed with it.
Let people follow one another without guile for the sake of mutual welfare.
I go for refuge to that supreme Dharma, wherein there is no mutual deception, in order to pursue it. || ū ||
I go alone for the sake of asceticism to create an island of all that is wholesome, free from all evil, with a pure mind.
I go for refuge indeed to that supreme Dharma, wherein there is no mutual deception, in order to pursue it. ||Ṛ||
Having perceived the truth, I shall return to the city;
accomplish your purpose, may it be well with you—farewell, I shall now depart.
I go for refuge indeed to that supreme Dharma, wherein there is no mutual deception, in order to pursue it. ||Ṛ||
Having thus instructed him and sent back his companion who was overwhelmed with grief,
Chandaka also departed on horseback and entered the joyless city.
Seeing the king along with his retinue, the royal ladies, and the cowherds all afflicted with distress, he spoke:
The firm-minded charioteer spoke these humble words in order to dispel his grief.
The charioteer, the people full of longing, the horse Citra, the excellent bow, and the entire devoted host— every one of them has been abandoned forever.
Having abandoned his people and kinsmen, he has gone forth to seek manifold virtues. (a)
Having attained the wholesome, he will return once more,
possessing fearlessness, the fruit of perfect peace, and utter purity.
Having abandoned his people and kinsmen, he has gone forth to seek manifold virtues. || Ā ||
The Creator shall surely make his unwavering power of intellect and valor, as well as his constant desire, fruitful.
Having abandoned his people and kinsmen, he has gone forth to seek manifold virtues. (8)
Seeking the welfare of people, have you gone forth as one solely intent on seeking their well-being, in order to make them free from sorrow?
Having abandoned his people and kinsmen, he has gone forth to seek manifold virtues. (II)
He has no fear, for he removes the fear of worldly existence;
though dwelling in the forest, he lives as if in a palace.
Having abandoned his virtuous father, the man has gone forth to seek many virtues. ||u||
Even animals bestow affection that is free from base impulses and devoid of fear.
Having abandoned his virtuous father, the man has gone forth to seek manifold virtues. ||ū||
Why should we worry for him?
He is always our provider of thought.
Having abandoned his virtuous kinsmen, he has gone forth to seek manifold virtues. ||Ṛ||
They have gone to obtain the wish-fulfilling gem;
he has gone to bring back the wish-fulfilling gem.
Having abandoned his people and kinsmen, he has gone forth to seek manifold virtues. ||ṛ||
When the king of auspicious mind had been thus awakened, he— along with his attendants, wife, and daughter-in-law— having attained some measure of well-being and desiring the welfare of all,
returned once more to see his son who had now attained the nectar of reality.
Though established in kingship, he constantly acted like one in the forest for the sake of pacifying the minds of the cowherds.
Having abandoned his kingdom and retired to the forest, he set his mind on peace;
going to a hermitage secluded from the world, he questioned the sages about reality;
then, having seen Ārāḍa and Udraka, those best of sages who had reached the further shore of the ocean of meditation, he strove [for liberation].
And salutations to you, who are intent on performing austerities together with groups of five ascetics.
Thus ends the sixth section, titled "The Great Departure," in the poem *Śrī Buddhodaya*, composed by the monk-scholar Śānti.
The Seventh Canto: The Practice of Austerity.
Having departed from his home, Gautama dismissed his attendants along with his wife and son.
"Though invited with half the kingdom by the Lord of Magadha, he remained free from passion;
desiring to attain the ultimate truth, he has come to this forest wishing to practice the supreme conduct"—thus did this report spread among the people, pervading the entire city of Urubilvā. (61)
Having learned the entire account from the son of Senānī, Sujātā—
desiring to purify herself through meritorious deeds arising from the service of the new sage—
performed supreme penance with great hardship, thereby leading her body toward its final transformation.
And other young maidens, having approached him, sang [this] with palms joined in reverence. ||62||
O Sujātā, dwell here according to your own practice; make the villages exceedingly excellent,
having attained glory through the imprint of your feet and being brought to a state worthy of worship.
This is the Vanī river, cooled by breezes from the Sallayana;
it has beautiful bathing-ghats and auspicious waters, flowing near our village. (a)
People will resort to your exceedingly pure fame that has spread abroad;
they will gather all the things required for your ascetic penance.
This forest, cooled by the breeze from the lake,
with its pure waters and excellent bathing-places, flows near our village with auspicious currents.
O virtuous lady, the trees with their dense shade, bearing fruit in due season,
and the trustworthy cowherds will provide for your hermitage.
This forest, cooled by the breeze from the healing waters, is the Nairañjanā river with its excellent bathing-places and auspicious currents, flowing near our village. II.
Indeed, these forest regions, which constitute my sphere of activity, are not devoid of predatory beasts;
they are filled with auspicious birds and deer and remain free from forest fires even in the summer.
This is the Vanī river, with its breeze that soothes;
the Nairañjanā, with its excellent bathing-places and auspicious waters, flows near our village. II.
During the day, wild young cowherd girls with their herds of cows are seen on the grassy meadows,
while other maidens are seen gathering wood in the dense forest.
This forest, cooled by the breeze from Lake Saṃlayana, with its auspicious waters and excellent bathing-ghats, lies near our village on the banks of the Nairañjanā. ||u||
There shall be no fear for you whatsoever, nor shall anyone cause you affliction as you move about here;
oh, what great fortune is ours! We offer you our constant salutations.
This forest, fanned by the breeze of healing, is the Nairañjanā river with its excellent bathing-places and auspicious waters, situated near our village. ||ū||
Solitude is easily found for you to perform austerities and practice meditation;
roam as you wish and wander always in this place free from obstacles.
This forest, fanned by the breeze of healing, is the Nairañjanā river with its excellent bathing-places and auspicious waters, situated near our village. ||Ṛ||
May it be that your sight is easily obtained by us as we approach,
so that we may perform service and salutation according to your convenience.
This forest is cooled by the breeze from the lake;
the Nairañjanā river, with its excellent bathing places and auspicious waters, flows near our village. ||Ṛ||
Perceiving the sage’s consent through his very silence, Sujātā, having respectfully served the sage for a moment and bowed down together with her five companions, departed;
may the attainment of truth come to me, who has taken refuge in this very forest grove.
Having thus resolved in his heart, he performed various austerities for six winters.

Though he was extremely faint from weakness and on the verge of death, even after performing austerities, he did not comprehend the reality; therefore, he perceived that this [path] was not the means for the true goal.
Thinking that the five [senses] would likewise depart from him who was intent on attaining physical health through coarse food, they withdrew elsewhere.
The group of five [disciples],
the renounced kingdom, the abandoned wife,
his kinsmen, and the Śākyas with their retinues.
It was not attained by one performing austerities;
how could the nectar of reality be obtained here by this man while he was eating? (a)
The sage Arāḍa, a hero among munis, was abandoned,
as was Udraka, though he was profound in meditation.
It was not attained by one performing austerities;
how could the nectar of reality be obtained here by this one who has merely eaten? || Ā ||
King Bimbisāra was abandoned by him,
even though he had offered half of his kingdom as a gift.
It was not attained by one performing austerities;
how could this nectar of reality be obtained here by one who has merely eaten? ||i||
Having abandoned the village, he has come to the forest; having come to a secluded place, he has come to practice asceticism.
It was not attained by one performing austerities;
how could the nectar of reality be obtained here by this man while he was eating? ||ī||
Attachment has been abandoned; he is absorbed in his own self.
Gross food has been abandoned; it is diminished.
If it was not attained by one performing austerities, nor by one who has already eaten, how could the nectar of reality be obtained here by this person? ||u||
Though his body was emaciated by asceticism,
that wise and radiant one did not attain the ultimate reality.
It was not attained by one performing austerities;
how could the nectar of reality be obtained here by this man while he was eating? ||ū||
Even his asceticism has now been abandoned;
not even the slightest truth will be accomplished by him now.
It was not attained by one performing austerities;
how could the nectar of reality be obtained here by this man while he was eating? ||ṛ||
We go from here elsewhere;
we dwell elsewhere than this.
It was not attained by one performing austerities;
how could the nectar of reality be obtained here by this man while he was eating? (Ṛ)
When they had thus departed, the sage Gautama,
accompanied by his own vigor, dwelt there devoted to solid food and regained the strength of his body as it was before.
Seeing him, who was pleasing to the eyes and eclipsing the splendor of the bodiless one with his own radiance, [the gods were amazed].
In that regard, people have given this great being the new designation of "śramaṇa. (65)

Having abandoned arduous austerities, she who was devoted to supreme meditative concentration and subsisted on almsfood arrived on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha; with a face like the full moon, spreading joy across the heart,
she prepared an extraordinary and peerless dish of milk-rice for that incomparable Gautama.
Having found him wandering for alms, she led him to her home and honored him with well-prepared food.
The commander’s daughter is peerless; the season in this land is peerless; Mādhava is peerless.
This food, prepared for my sake, is held in a peerless golden vessel.
The food is noble milk-rice, peerless; the consecrated worship is peerless.
And having eaten this, he will undoubtedly attain the peerless state today. || 67 ||
Thus reflecting in his heart,

he remembered her former manifold worship, as well as that auspicious woman— virtuous, with joined palms, bowed in reverence, offering incomparable sacrificial food, beautiful, and desiring his welfare.
Gautama made her joyful with all his heart through these meritorious words.
The Great Śramaṇa will cause your worship to bear excellent fruit;
your worship will lead to your spiritual welfare.
"This which has been brought forth is like nectar;
having obtained this nectar that was to be attained, my doubt has been dispelled."
Desiring my welfare and desiring my prosperity,
may you become one whose desires have borne fruit.
"This [instruction] brought forth is like nectar;
having consumed this nectar that is to be attained, my doubt has been dispelled. ||a||
You are my supreme companion in the Dharma;
you are my supreme companion in virtue;
[this] which has been brought forth is like nectar.
Having consumed this nectar that was to be attained, my doubt has been dispelled. ||i||
My five companions have also departed;
you alone remain as my companion along with your sisters.
This [teaching] brought forth is like nectar;
having tasted this nectar that is to be attained, my doubt has been dispelled. ||ī||
While you were engaged in difficult austerities, you protected your body even when it had fallen into a state of doubt.
This which has been brought forth is like nectar;
having partaken of this nectar that is to be attained, my doubt has been dispelled. ||u||
These vital breaths of yours are sustained by these soups;
these vital breaths of yours are maintained by these soups.
This [teaching] brought forth is like nectar;
having attained this nectar that is to be realized, my doubt has been dispelled. ||ū||
Your form was lost through arduous asceticism;
by serving you, it has been regained once more.
This [teaching] brought forth is like nectar;
having attained this nectar, my doubt has been dispelled. ||Ṛ||
Today, by the power of your food, I shall be victorious;
I shall even bring Māra under my control.
This [teaching] has been presented as comparable to nectar;
having obtained this nectar that was to be attained, my doubt has been dispelled. ||Ṛ||
Having spoken thus, the sage took the stainless vessel of supreme food in his hand,
approached the riverbank, and with a joyful mind ate that milk-rice. Having eaten, he attained full strength of body and mind, and with a serene interior, he remained.
The bowl was made of gold; its purpose being understood, he cast it into the current of the river.
Having enjoyed the discourse on Dharma delivered by his mouth to Sujātā— who stood on the bank, supremely filled with devotion, radiant with virtues, and now delighted—
he departed; one woman, having bowed to him with respect, quickly went to her own home.
And another, wise and moving with the playful gait of a lion-king, set out for the Bodhi tree. || 70 ||
Thus ends the seventh episode, titled "The Practice of Austerities," in the poem *Śrī Buddhodaya* composed by Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī.
The eighth episode: Victory over Māra.
Having respectfully spread out a seat of auspicious grass arranged in the form of a svastika, he sat down.
The ascetic bound a firm cross-legged posture at the Bodhi tree for the sake of enlightenment;
then Brahmā and the other gods rejoiced with well-disposed minds, and the earth trembled with joy,
while Māra, his mind already distressed by that ascetic’s penance, now gave way to rage.
He had approached the foot of the tree together with Rati, surrounded by beautiful women,
and was attended by terrifying beings with hideous faces holding weapons in their hands,
who were intent on causing various kinds of frightening disturbances to him as he was striving for awakening.
The peaceful gods, in order to subdue that Māra who was blinded by rage, spoke thus: || 72 ||
For no woman, however shapely, can cause such intoxication in the heart of a child;
rather, it is the child who has the power to bring delight to the minds of young women.
Desist from this resolve, Māra—from this most despicable means accompanied by lust and violence. ||a||
Seeing this, the daughters of Māra might have felt passion;
yet, being themselves abashed by his beauty, they would not produce even a gesture of love.
"Desist from this resolve, Māra! From this most contemptible means accompanied by lust and violence! ||a||
I suspect that, in order to find him,
these women will perform penances, smeared with ashes and even discarding their divine unguents.
Desist from this resolve, Māra; from this most contemptible means accompanied by lust and violence. ||i||
Formerly attached to his form, they will later abandon you to seek refuge with him in order to worship him and achieve their own welfare.
Desist from this resolve, Māra; [desist] from this most contemptible means accompanied by lust and violence. ||ī||
Thus, being without retinue, even Rati will abandon you as you burn him,
in order to go and worship that wise one.
Desist from this resolve, Māra; from this most contemptible means accompanied by lust and violence! ||u||
These predatory creatures are useless; what could they possibly do?
Yet, if they were to approach his presence, they would attain a state of gentleness.
Desist from this resolve, Māra; [desist] from this most contemptible means accompanied by lust and violence. ||ū||
Tell me, what kind of blow will you inflict with your flower-arrows?
Go, gather flowers and offer him your prostration.
Desist from this resolve, Māra; [desist] from this most contemptible means accompanied by lust and violence. ||ṛ||
Free from all desires, abstaining from violence, and being the gateway to merit—
approach that [state] with compassion and resort to it again and again.
Desist from this resolve, Māra; [desist] from this most contemptible means accompanied by lust and violence. ||ṛ||
Though thus awakened, he remained enraged; casting a multitude of flower-arrows and even with divine missiles and playful charms, he sought to agitate his heart,
repeatedly terrifying him at night with swarms of predatory beasts.
As if exhausted at the end, falling upon the earth, he was held up by Rati with both her hands. || 73 ||

Seeing her own progenitor defeated, the unconquered Rati was herself defeated; beholding him trembling, she was terrified and shaken by fear. Seeing Madana regain some consciousness, she too regained her senses.
Having bowed to the steadfast one who had reached the further shore of enlightenment, those noble women, with tears and their hair standing on end, spoke thus: 74.
You are delight; you are the refuge; your word is the refuge; we have come for refuge.
Your speech, endowed with its full perfection, possesses the quality of removing afflictions.
Victory to you, O treasury of Dharma!
Victory, victory to you, O possessor of peaceful intent, O source of compassion, O ordainer of welfare and security!
What need is there for words? By your silence you give us that by which we are fully satisfied;
now we have obtained great wealth, whereas previously we were merely robbed.
Victory to you, O treasury of Dharma! Victory, victory to you, O one of peaceful mind, O maker of compassion, O ordainer of welfare and security! Āḥ!
You are the jewel of the world; through you alone among all people are we possessed of jewels.
To worship you, the very jewel, we are always ever-striving.
Victory to you, O treasury of Dharma! Victory, victory to you, O one of peaceful mind, O maker of compassion, O ordainer of welfare and security! i||
O Compassionate One, look upon us for a single moment with your merciful gaze;
make our one small merit bear fruit, and render our many misdeeds fruitless.
Victory to You, O Treasure of Dharma!
Victory, victory to you, O Śāntimati, O source of compassion, O ordainer of welfare and security! ||ī||
O Lord, even the offense committed by us brings you delight;
for even the mischievous play of young children brings joy to their parents.
Victory to you, O treasury of Dharma! Victory, victory to you, O possessor of peaceful intent, O maker of compassion, O ordainer of welfare and security! ||u||
Even our ill-spoken words shall not produce distress in you;
for the heat of a firefly never causes fever, even though it produces warmth.
Victory to you, O treasury of Dharma! Victory, victory to you, O possessor of peaceful intent, O creator of compassion, O ordainer of welfare and security! ||ū||
May even this misdeed committed in play lead to joy,
just as the distress of the summer heat brings about a downpour of rain.
Victory to you, O treasury of Dharma! Victory, victory to you, O possessor of peaceful intent, O mine of compassion, O ordainer of welfare and security! (Ṛ)
With palms joined in reverence, this salutation is offered to you; may it remove our sins, generate merit that brings about the abundance of happiness, and dispel all suffering.
Victory to you, O treasury of Dharma! Victory, victory to you, O possessor of peaceful intent, O maker of compassion, O ordainer of welfare and security! ||Ṛ||

Having bowed to the Bodhisattva, the Māras, surrounded by their wives and accompanied by arrogant soldiers, departed with their hands raised; Rati, her passion released by anger, went away out of shame.
Alone at the foot of the tree, the Conqueror of Māra was hailed by Brahmā and the other gods.
Free from obstacles and devoted to meditation within his heart, he remained steadfast for the sake of perfect enlightenment. ||75||

At the onset of night, he first entered upon his succession of previous births; then, with his divine vision, he perceived this entire world— including its human beings— as unstable by the very nature of cyclic existence,
seeing sentient beings subject to birth, old age, calamity, and death.
In that middle watch of the night, I mastered the authoritative knowledge that "all is suffering."
Suffering is the fruit of birth, and this birth arises from grasping produced by existence; if craving grasps at sense objects, that craving originates from sensation;
sensation occurs by the power of contact, which arises from the six sense bases, which in turn emerge from name-and-form.
Furthermore, this arising of consciousness occurs again and again from formative forces through ignorance. (77)
Thus, the entire succession of suffering for all living beings revolves;
indeed, it would be completely overturned through the obstruction of ignorance.
Here, there is no self as a real entity, nor is there any cognition that has a single locus, nor is there any volitional action.
This very self and this world are nothing but the transformation of the aggregates (skandhas). 78.

The path, when practiced by one who is without companion, which is free from the afflictions of enjoyment and serves to destroy the succession of sufferings— that is virtuous, capable of yoga, and middling. And thus, that suchness which is devoid of self and non-self has been attained by me through my excellence.
The night has passed; this light-maker has arisen. I have now become awakened.
The Buddha is the vision regarding suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path;
for one who possesses knowledge of these as they truly are, there is a constant rain of happiness therein.
Awakening is non-awakening, utterly pure;
the entire succession of sufferings has this very day been brought to cessation. ||a||
For he who is endowed with freedom from desire, free from violence and malice,
and whose intention is constant— such a person becomes liberated from suffering.
Awakening is non-awakening, utterly pure;
the entire succession of sufferings has been ceased this very day. ||a||
For one who abstains from false speech, harsh words, slander, and divisive talk, right speech arises; for one who does not abstain from these, joy does not arise.
Awakening is non-awakening, utterly pure;
