the entire succession of sufferings has been brought to cessation this very day. ||i||
He who does not commit the evil deeds of taking life, stealing the property of others, or sexual misconduct—happiness belongs to him alone; it is his own well-done deed that has been accomplished.
Awakening is non-awakening, utterly pure;
the entire succession of sufferings has been brought to cessation this very day. ||ī||
He who does not engage in that worldly activity by which violence is produced,
and who abstains from intoxicants, weapons, animals, and slaughterhouses— he goes to the further shore.
Awakening is non-awakening, utterly pure;
the entire succession of sufferings has been brought to cessation this very day. ||u||
He who exerts right effort toward the wholesome and increases his virtue is happy; he whose mind does not incline toward the unwholesome and who avoids what is unwholesome is likewise happy.
Awakening is non-awakening, utterly pure;
the entire succession of sufferings has been completely ceased this very day. ||ū||
He who is not deluded by pleasure and pain within a defiled body is well-yoked; he who does not fall under the sway of the body, the senses, and the mind—which are ever-restless—is liberated.
Awakening is non-awakening, utterly pure;
the entire succession of sufferings has this very day been brought to cessation. ||Ṛ||
He who makes the mind one-pointed and endowed with loving-kindness and compassion, he truly awakens; he sleeps in peace and attains a state liberated from suffering.
Awakening is non-awakening, utterly pure;
the entire succession of sufferings has been ceased this very day. ||ṛ||
To him who cultivates the path with a liberated mind, who is devoted to the practice of compassion,
and who accepts the auspicious honey offered during alms by the brothers Madhu and Bhallika;
to him who makes the nectar of Brahma’s prayer melodious like a nightingale’s song.
We pay homage to the Buddha, the glorious one who has conquered the enemy body. 80.
Thus ends the eighth episode, titled "The Victory over Māra," in the poem *Śrī Buddhodaya* composed by the monk-scholar Śānti.
The ninth section:
The establishment of the Saṅgha;
in the month of Āṣāḍha, the Jina turned the Wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park.

In Kāśī, this host of five sages—who were led by Kauṇḍinya and established by the Conqueror of Smara for the sake of the welfare and happiness of the worlds—was maintained by Him in the fourfold Noble Truths; yet now, it is turning toward the absence of completeness. 81.
Dharma does not discriminate based on birth; Dharma regards only virtues.
Through Dharma, a person here attains the state of the noble; he who possesses Dharma is twice-born (*dvija*).
Dharma, having set aside distinctions among the multitudes of men, brings them to a single lineage.
A wondrous sound concerning the refuge of the Sugata was heard echoing in every direction. || 82 ||

The Dharma has been attained by Brahmins and Śūdras, by those who are low, high, or middling among the worlds, and by those of various speech, colors, and forms, whether they be yellow, white, or black.
All of them were compassionate in their inner hearts, devoted to helping one another; even those who enjoyed only a little food attained the supreme bliss of awakening in every respect. 83.
The Saṅgha is devoted to the Dharma, a son of the Victor, homeless, free from craving, subsisting on alms, intent here upon renouncing even the three robes,
wise, and skilled in the gift of knowledge; through compassion, by way of the training in the totality [of the path],...
He ordained a single auspicious human nature, which is the sole nest for the entire universe.
That group of householders in this world, who have completely cast off the impure conceptualizations of fools such as livelihood and the like,

who possess an intellect that perceives no distinction between themselves and others in the assembly or the row, and who are liberated from grasping at caste in their own conduct— [they alone are worthy].
He made all the people of the earth bound by kinship and united into a single lineage. ||85||
Where women are like men, where wives are as open as daughters, where there is no tormenting by birth-status, and where the astrologer’s false views do not cause defilement—
there the entire mode of livelihood is considered right through compassion and non-violence.
The followers of the Sugata are established in that Dharma, which has as its supreme goal the singular aim of benefiting the world. || 86 ||
One whose mind has attained liberation strives diligently in this Dharma; another, wise, dispassionate, and gentle, practices a pure livelihood through non-violence while remaining at home.
Yet another man, a virtuous soul for whom liberation is supreme, abandons his home along with his wife.
The wise man, intent on renunciation, wanders for his livelihood solely by means of alms. || 87 ||
He moves about, abstaining from improper conduct because he is weary of this impurity of the Kali age, remaining far removed from passion;
and he does so with a flood of compassion, thinking, "All people are like me."
He practices, abstaining from unwholesome deeds;
having severed each fetter one by one, he delights in the security of awakening.
The undeluded one constantly practices this conditionality and takes refuge in the Three Jewels.
He practices, abstaining from what is unwholesome;
having severed each fetter one by one, he delights in the security of enlightenment. ||a||
The wise man, having pierced through the three ends and not the heresy,
has emerged from the cosmic egg.
He practices, abstaining from unwholesome deeds; having severed each of the fetters, he delights in the security of enlightenment. (i)
One standing on high looks down;
even one afflicted by passion goes upward.
He practices, abstaining from unwholesome deeds;
having severed each of the fetters, he delights in the security of awakening. (8)
He goes higher and higher and ever higher;
he looks downward and does not descend.
He practices, abstaining from unwholesome deeds;
having severed each fetter one by one, he delights in the security of enlightenment. ||u||
Though risen to a high position, he does not become attached;
though fallen to a low position, he becomes detached from both the high and the low.
He practices, abstaining from unwholesome deeds;
having severed each fetter one by one, he delights in the security of awakening. ||ū||
When passion has ceased, the mind is at peace;
when the sense of "mine" is absent, the intellect is tranquil;
one who abstains from unwholesome conduct proceeds [toward liberation].
Having severed each fetter one by one, he delights in the security of enlightenment. ||ṛ||
The conceit of "Who am I? has vanished;
the dawning of true knowledge has occurred.
He practices, abstaining from unwholesome deeds;
having severed each fetter one by one, he delights in the security of enlightenment. ||ṛ||
For one who has attained nirvāṇa through the destruction of afflictions, there is no higher abode nor any limitation of place or time;
having drunk the nectar of liberation, he is successful in every way and happy.
Others, however, hold the view that liberation is merely tasteless; [the wise man], devoted to the welfare of all, is otherwise.
Exerting himself, the son of the Buddha, whose supreme goal is the Buddha, proceeds here toward enlightenment. ||88||
When one person has crossed over [to liberation], what fruit does he ripen for himself? He enjoys it by himself and gives nothing to another;
thus, one who seeks only his own interest does not become a creator of fortune for all people.
What is the fruit for one who has crossed over alone, when everyone else remains submerged? And what is the fruit for one who has reached the further shore, if [the others] have not? (a)
What is the use of that morality which has been proclaimed for one whose mind does not know how to benefit others, yet who goes to dwell in solitude merely to protect himself from suffering?
"What is the fruit for one who has crossed alone, when all are submerged? And what is the fruit for one who has reached the further shore? (A)
Having established friendliness toward the trees in the solitary forest, his lifespan increased through asceticism;
ever patient and worthy of honor, he was indeed a shrine, but not a human being.
What is the fruit for one who has crossed alone, when all are submerged? And what is the fruit for one who has reached the further shore? ||i||
What is not achieved by him who displays the state of a hero, who disregards the welfare of others here and acts only for his own sake? Everyone does exactly that for themselves.
What is the fruit for one who has crossed alone when everyone else remains submerged? And what is the fruit even for one who has reached the further shore? ||9||
Why does our mind, already solitary and protected by the bliss of meditation, turn toward further solitude,
even abandoning the Protector of the World?
What is the fruit for one who has crossed alone, when all are submerged? And what is the fruit for one who has reached the further shore alone? ||u||
Of what use is that one who is liberated through knowledge to us in this world bound by fetters—
he who, while the entire world is in sorrow, remains free from grief and lacks the capacity for compassion?
What is the fruit for one who has crossed over alone, when all are submerged? And what is the fruit for one who has reached the further shore alone? ||9||
He whose well-earned wealth is for the sake of others, and whose body is for the sake of others—that hero is indeed a great hero; I truly salute that preeminent hero.
What is the fruit for one who has crossed alone, when all are submerged? And what is the fruit for one who has reached the further shore? || Ṛ ||
I bow to the noble one who, though possessing nothing and dwelling in solitude, has renounced both women and gold;
who is forever free from craving and whose virtuous deeds are honored like sacred shrines.
What is the fruit for one who has crossed over alone, when everyone else remains submerged? And what is the fruit for one who has reached the further shore, if all have likewise reached it? ||ṛ||

Those virtuous ones who are free from attachment, who have attained the state of having fulfilled their duties, who are devoid of craving, or those who are devoted to helping others and look toward the world—they both, day after day, offer this blessing to these two classes of people: "May you never lack the means of subsistence; may you always be free from disease; may you always be intent on the welfare of others; and may you always be devoted to the service of the virtuous."
May this blessing be fulfilled; may there be auspiciousness for all worlds throughout existence. ||89||
May the righteous-minded king be established;
may the earth, nourished by rivers, shine forth as a giver of happiness and abundant harvests;
may the deity send rain in due season; and may the instruction of righteousness spread throughout the world.
May the king be righteous in soul;
may all the subjects also be intent on dharma and mutually well-disposed toward one another. ||a||
May the Teacher become the lord of the worlds, bestowing prosperity upon them through righteousness alone, without punishment and without the sword.
"May the king be righteous;
may all the subjects also be intent upon dharma and devoted to one another's welfare. ||a||
May there be a cessation of war in this world; may peace spread across the earth;
and may the world abstain from the slaughter of living beings and from the consumption of meat.
May the king be righteous in soul;
may all the subjects also be intent on dharma and devoted to one another's welfare. (1)
May houses have their doors wide open; may theft depart from people;
and may food, drink, medicine, clothing, and dwellings attain abundance.
May the king be righteous in soul;
may all the subjects also be intent on dharma and mutually well-disposed toward one another. ||8||
Let women move about freely and without fear, along with their children and daughters, full of joy;
let neither men nor women act wantonly, but remain equally disciplined.
May the king be righteous in soul;
may all the subjects also be intent on dharma and mutually well-disposed toward one another. ||u||
Let the people here be speakers of truth, finding delight in truth, conducting themselves solely by truth, assisting one another, and dwelling in peace.
May the king be righteous in soul;
may all the subjects also be intent upon dharma and be well-disposed toward one another. ||ū||
May everyone, having abandoned that which robs the intellect, causes evil, and through which the world becomes intoxicated— that intoxicant— be happy and free from sorrow.
May the king be righteous in soul;
may all the subjects also be intent on dharma and mutually well-disposed toward one another. ||Ṛ||
May there be welfare for the world of people; may the assembly be auspicious.
May the friendship be accomplished and auspicious; may auspicious speech be successful.
May the head of state be righteous-souled.
May all the people of the kingdom also be righteous-minded and intent on each other's welfare. ||ṛ||
They extend the hermitage of conduct for the welfare and happiness of the entire world; having attained the auspicious state, they teach the entirety of the Dharma;
and through their excellent speech, they make the vast collection of the Buddha’s teachings flourish.
We pay homage to the Buddha, whose mind has attained the sublime, and to the Saṅgha. || 90 ||
Thus ends the ninth episode, titled "The Establishment of the Saṅgha," in the poem *Śrī Buddhodaya* composed by the monk-scholar Śānti.
The tenth chapter:
The characteristics of the Buddha-body;
having fulfilled [his perfections] in Lumbinī, he delighted his kinsmen with his childhood deeds.
Having seen the world as impure, he abandoned all [attachments] and performed difficult austerities;

having partaken on the full moon day of Vaiśākha of the excellent milk-rice offered by Sujātā, that Blessed One attained enlightenment and, being perfectly at peace, may he protect us while teaching the Dharma. 91.
He who was directly perceived for eighty autumns preached the Dharma for the benefit of the world with his emanation body for fifty years;
thereafter, he was remembered and honored by means of countless stupas constructed over his relics.
May the Blessed Buddha, with his [images] and variegated paintings, ordain our well-being. 92.

The Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks and the eighteen glorious secondary characteristics, whose nature is that of the Sambhogakāya, is beyond the reach of ordinary perception even for children;
yet all the poets of the world combined would not be able to fully describe his delightful splendor.
Though he is sung of only by a fraction of his glory, may he bring happiness to us, who are fortunate. || 93 ||
I bow to the Giver of Boons, who possesses the most excellent marks, who stands tall while bowing, and who is honored by all the world;
I touch your lotus-feet, which are ever celebrated by the virtuous.
I bow to the Blessed One, the granter of boons, who possesses the most excellent marks;
oh, what great fortune it is for me that I approach him while beholding him! ||a||
I stand here fearless and free from fever, in your hand which protects the three worlds, which possesses auspicious marks, and which is devoted to compassion and acts as a source of mercy.
I bow to the Blessed One, the granter of boons, who possesses the most excellent marks;
oh, what great fortune it is for me that I approach him while beholding him! ||a||
O you who possess eyes like full-blown lotuses, who dispel my entire web of grief and suffering with a mere glance, and who are so enchanting as to captivate the mind!
I bow to the Blessed One, the granter of boons, who possesses the most excellent marks;
oh, what my good fortune, that I come here beholding him! ||i||
May that beautiful face, resembling a lotus with a blue bee,
bestow physical well-being upon my body and bestow happiness upon my mind.
I bow to the Blessed One, the granter of boons, who possesses the most excellent marks;
oh, what great fortune it is for me that I approach him while beholding him!
May the eyebrow between your eyebrows, marked by a clockwise curl,
fulfill my heart's desire and grant my mind’s longing.
I bow to the Blessed One, the granter of boons, who possesses the most excellent marks;
oh, what great fortune it is for me that I approach him while beholding him! ||u||
May she, whose skin is more beautiful than the moon, who is the delight of Rati’s heart,
and who removes the fever of my passion, be forever praised by me.
I bow to the Blessed One, the granter of boons, who possesses the most excellent marks;
oh, what great fortune it is for me that I approach him while beholding him! ||ū||
May He whose body is golden-hued, who grasps at nothing but pure compassion,
and who by nature is free from all attachment, bestow every auspiciousness.
I bow to the Blessed One, the granter of boons, who possesses the most excellent marks;
oh, what great fortune it is for me that I approach him while beholding him! ||ṛ||
I hold in my mind the Jina, who possesses the characteristics of a pleasing form, the characteristics of being sublime and complete, who is most auspicious and endowed with excellent marks.
I bow to the Blessed One, the giver of boons, who possesses the most excellent marks;
oh, what great fortune it is for me that I approach him while beholding him! ||ṛ||
While the Blessed One, the best among speakers, remained in the state of silence through his manifested body,
yet abandoned solitude to undertake a journey together with his disciples,
those well-spoken words which he uttered while standing in the midst of the assembly—
May those [teachings], which are solely devoted to the single goal of peace, be all the more effective for our well-being. || 94 ||
This entire collection of well-spoken verses has been composed for the welfare and happiness of many people; it fulfills all the desires of men,
pacifies every evil, is filled with auspiciousness, and is seen to be meaningful in its purpose.
All that is well-spoken has been done;
whatever well-spoken words exist here, all of them have been spoken by the Jina. (a)
Impelled by great compassion, it is entirely pure, endowed with all that is righteous,
esteemed by the virtuous, free from the sense of duality, possessed of excellent qualities, and delightful.
All that is well-spoken has been done;
whatever well-spoken word exists here, all of that was spoken by the Jina. ||a||
It is free from all craving for sensual desires, it brings about the pacification of the afflictions, it establishes one in the constant practice of right conduct, and it dispels wrong conduct.
All that is well-spoken has been done;
whatever well-spoken word exists here, all of that was spoken by the Jina. ||i||
Having cast far away passion for the objects of the form-dhyānas, it is free from attachment;
it dispels the addiction to the pleasures of meditation and partakes in the portion of most pure qualities.
All that is well-spoken has been done;
whatever well-spoken word exists here, all that was spoken by the Jina. ||ī||
Just as one instructs an actor on the stage regarding the worlds of form and the desire-realm,
he taught here that, like desire, attachment to form must be pacified within the formless.
All that is well-spoken has been done;
whatever well-spoken words exist here, all of them have been spoken by the Jina. ||u||
It brings about peace and its benefits, removes delusion, is devoted to non-violence,
and desists from the misfortune of evil, such as killing, binding, violent combat, strife, and defilement.
All that is well-spoken has been done [by the Buddha];
whatever well-spoken word exists here, all of it was spoken by the Jina. ||ū||
Then he praised supreme silence, supreme detachment, and that which is most profound—
devoid of all possessions and revered by the wise.
All that is well-spoken has been done;
whatever well-spoken word exists here, all that was spoken by the Jina. (Ṛ)
Free from distinctions of caste, lineage, family, language, or complexion, he is steadfast;
like unto himself, he acts for the welfare of others, being profound and composed of the essence of compassion.
All that is well-spoken has been done;
whatever well-spoken word exists here, all of that was spoken by the Jina. ||ṝ||
He who is eternally established here in the form of his own dharma, possessing activity and true qualities,
is declared to be devoid of activity and lacking qualities once conceptualization has ceased;
he is the Blessed One, Gautama Śauddhodani, whose very manifestation is a creative emanation.
May that Jina, the perfected one among those who know reality, protect us from misfortune. 95.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One;
though free from passion here, you have conquered the world that is full of passion. Being yourself sorrowless, you have removed the sorrow of these men.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, who, though devoid of qualities and free from defects, is always possessed of every excellence. ||a||
Having approached you, even one who is angry becomes joyful in an instant;
O contented one, you have conquered the wrathful with a mind that has conquered anger.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One,
who, though devoid of qualities and free from defects, is always possessed of every excellence.
Ignorance deludes the world when you are not perceived directly;
yet as the presiding lord of knowledge, you have awakened the deluded through the word of wisdom.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, who, though devoid of qualities and free from defects, is always possessed of every excellence. ||i||
Completely free from rivalry, you are the eldest among the worlds;
though you move about with impartiality, you are peerless and the most excellent of all.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, who, though devoid of qualities and free from defects, is always possessed of every excellence. ||ī||
Among all visible things, your form is a jewel that subdues the intoxication of passion;
it produces purity within the heart and pacifies the defilement of every worldly affliction.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, who, though devoid of qualities and free from defects, is always possessed of every excellence. ||u||
Whatever you speak, people listen to it with attentive minds and great effort;
for your speech is the best among all that is worth hearing, becoming a jewel of well-spoken words.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, who, though devoid of [worldly] qualities and free from defects, is eternally possessed of every excellence. ||ū||
The wise revere that Dharma which has been taught by you; the foolish, however, bow with devotion and pay homage to that which is upheld by the Tripiṭaka.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, who, though devoid of qualities and free from defects, is always possessed of every excellence. ||ṛ||
You are the sustainer of those qualities of the Dharma—loving-kindness, wisdom, and dispassion.
Victory, victory, O Lord! You are the ordainer of good fortune for those who are without a protector.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, who, though devoid of qualities and free from defects, is eternally possessed of every excellence. ||ṛ||

Having first seen the birth of the fortunate one among the Śākya people, then his upbringing through enjoyments, and through his skillfulness his attainment of Yaśodharā; having then observed the omens, his departure from the home, his conquest of Māra, and his attainment of supreme enlightenment—
And may that which is shown by the Blessed One, which finds its fulfillment in the establishment of the Dharma, protect us! 96.
At whose request this poem was composed by me in verses worthy of being sung;
who, longing for him, rejoices at this supreme moment attained through it;
and who, adorned with the glory of awakening, is my friend in my domestic life.
This well-born woman joyfully recites this poem offered to me with happiness. 97.

Desiring to sing in its entirety the life-story of the Tathāgata— which provides a refuge that is firm and serene through well-spoken words for people blinded by passion, which dispels the exhaustion of the mind, and which cuts off the intoxication of desire— I myself [undertake this].
This poem, whose sole essence is peace, has been composed by a poet who is devoted to the Buddha. 98.
Delightful is the state of a Buddha; delightful is the Buddha’s discourse consisting of well-spoken words;
delightful is the eloquence of poetry, endowed with virtuous qualities and accompanied by songs of verse.
Delightful is the essence of devotion, which takes refuge in Śauddhodani, the supreme teacher of the world.
May my composition become beautiful by resorting to that which is beautiful. || 99 ||
O Lord Śākyasiṃha, this [work] is beautiful through its accounts of conduct and the praise of beautiful qualities;
it is beautiful as a new elixir of devotion arising with sweetness,
even when compared to the beautiful and sovereign compositions of ancient and skilled poets.
"Ah, the virtuous, out of affection, describe the arising of wisdom as 'delightful, truly delightful'! || 100 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Buddha-body," in the poem *Śrī-Buddhodaya* composed by the monk-scholar Śānti.
The poem *Śrī-Buddhodaya* is hereby completed. This work is the composition of the monk-scholar Śānti.
[Colophon] In the incomparable Avadāna of Prajñā, on the island of Siṃhala,
and here in another monastery of the Sugatas renowned by the name Vidyālaṃkāra.

May this poem entitled *Buddhodaya*, composed by the twice-born Śrī Śāntibhikṣu— who was initiated into the excellent doctrine of the Śramaṇas by the venerable Śrī Dharmānanda— attain its rightful place among the virtuous.

Thus, [this work] was composed by the disciple of the venerable Śrī Dharmānandana Ācāryapāda, who had lived abroad in Siṃhala with his wife and son, and who now resides in the village of Bībīpur near Lakṣmaṇapura in Kosala in Northern India;
he is a recipient of the degree of Doctor from Lā-i P’chig University and holds the title of Vidyalamkāra at Viśvavidyālaya.

This is the work of the great master of Sanskrit, the scholar and venerable Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrin, Sāhityācārya: the poem entitled *Buddhodaya*, adorned with the life-story of the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme teacher of the entire world; it is a source of the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhaktirasa*), charming with the beauty of the subject matter—the Tathāgata, the most excellent hero, Śāntanātha. May there be auspiciousness!
